title: First teachers
hookLine: parents are called first teachers, worthy of honor (Itivuttaka 106)

lines: WHO TAUGHT YOU TO HOLD A SPOON?
cards: Who taught you to hold a spoon? Nobody remembers the lesson, but somebody gave it, probably more than once, probably with a towel nearby.
Before any school, any book, any teacher with a title, there was a pair of hands showing you how the world works: this is hot, this is a cat, this is how you say thank you.
One short discourse in the Itivuttaka gives those hands a name. It gives them a teacher's title.

teach.h: MOTHER AND FATHER, HONORED AT HOME
teach.b: In Itivuttaka 106, the Buddha says that a family where mother and father are honored at home lives with Brahma, the high god of that world. It lives with the first teachers. It lives with those worthy of gifts.
These, he says, are terms for mother and father. And he gives the reason in one plain sentence, paraphrased here: parents do much for their children.

teach.h: THEY SHOW THEIR CHILDREN THIS WORLD
teach.b: They bring them up, they feed them, and they show them this world. Show them this world: that's the job description of a first teacher. Not doctrine, not scripture.
The world itself: a face, a word, a door, a road.
The Pali for first teachers is pubbacariya: pubba, earlier, and acariya, teacher. A teacher's title, and here it goes to the people in the kitchen. The verse at the end gets practical.

teach.h: FOOD, CLOTHES, A PLACE TO REST
teach.b: The wise honor them with food and drink, with clothes and a place to sleep, by bathing them and washing their feet. Care for the body that once cared for yours. Two honest things belong beside this text.
First, it speaks of parents as they are meant to be, the ones who raise, feed and show. Not everyone had that, and the text doesn't pretend to describe every home.
Some Buddhist teachers widen it to whoever did that work for you: a grandmother, an aunt, a neighbor, a foster parent.

Second, the same idea runs through the Buddha's teaching to Sigala, where a grown child supports the parents who once supported them. Honor, here, isn't a feeling first. It's food, clothing, a place to rest.

how: In some Buddhist households, especially in Theravada countries, children bow to their parents on special days, and families make offerings or give food to monks in their parents' names as a way of honoring them.

o: parents, who show children this world
the earliest disciples of the Buddha
the monks who teach new novices

p: food, clothes, a place to rest

s: Itivuttaka 106 gives parents the title first teachers
among the high names he gives mother and father are Brahma, first teachers, and worthy of gifts.
the discourse says honor is only a feeling of respect
its verse names food and drink, clothing, bedding, bathing and washing the feet.
the same care for parents appears in the teaching to Sigala
there a grown child supports the parents who once supported them.

games.q: the Buddha gives parents high titles, Brahma and first teachers among them. what reason does he give?
o: they are older than their children.
they bring up, feed, and show their children this world.
games.why: the reason is the work they did: raising, feeding, and showing the child the world. the honor follows the care.

practice: Bring to mind one person who showed you this world when you were small: a parent, if that's who it was, or a grandparent, an elder, anyone who fed you and named things for you.
Picture one ordinary thing they taught you, the spoon, the shoelace, the way to say sorry, and let a quiet thank you sit in the chest. If they're gone, the thanks can stay right here.

wordCard.voice: First teachers. Pubbacariya: in Itivuttaka 106, a name for mother and father, who raise, feed, and show their children this world. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali pubbacariya: first or earliest teacher, from pubba, earlier, and acariya, teacher.

carryVoice: Your line: show them this world. Before any school, there were first teachers. Day six hundred thirty-two.
